pages.title: COHOMOLOGY OF EXCELLENT PRESCHEMES OF EQUAL CHARACTERISTIC

blocks.html:
EXPOSÉ XIX
COHOMOLOGY OF EXCELLENT PRESCHEMES OF EQUAL CHARACTERISTICby M. Artin
Contents

1. Purity for the ring \(k[[x_1, \ldots, x_n]]\).
2. The case of a strictly local ring.
3. Purity.
4. Local acyclicity of a regular morphism.
5. Finiteness theorem.
6. Cohomological dimension of affine morphisms.
7. Affine morphisms – end of the proof.

In this exposé we develop the theory of étale cohomology for excellent preschemes (EGA IV 7.8.1) of equal characteristic, assuming the theorem of resolution of singularities for such preschemes, in the following form:

Let \(X = \operatorname{Spec} A\) be an excellent local scheme of equal characteristic, and let \(U \subset X\) be a regular open set. There exists a proper birational morphism \(f : X' \to X\) and an open immersion \(U \to X'\) over \(X\) such that \(X'\) is regular and \(Y = X - U\) is everywhere of codimension \(1\), with transversal intersections.
The proofs are therefore valid, "for the time being", only in characteristic zero [4]. One could also deduce from them results for preschemes of characteristic \(p > 0\) in low dimensions [1].

Under the hypothesis of resolution, one obtains more or less satisfactory results for preschemes of equal characteristic and for coefficients prime to the characteristic (cf. 3.2, 4.1, 5.1, 6.1). By contrast, almost nothing is known about the cohomology of general preschemes of unequal characteristic, even in dimension 2, where resolution is available [2]. For example, the purity theorem 2.1 is not known for any complete ring of unequal characteristic of dimension \(> 1\). This result, for the rings of formal power series \(k[[x_1, \ldots, x_n]]\) (1.2), is one of the principal tools in the theory. Let us note moreover that the proof of 1.2 does not use the resolution theorem. This theorem is thus proved in arbitrary characteristic.

We shall often use, without explicit mention, the properties of excellent schemes developed in EGA IV 7.8, such as stability under extensions of finite type (EGA IV 7.8.3 (ii)) and under strict localizations. This last fact results from resolution and from EGA IV 7.9.5.
1. Purity for the ring \(k[[x_1, \ldots, x_n]]\).
Let us recall the following corollary of XVI 3.7:

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 1.1

Let \(A\) be a strictly local ring, and denote by \(A\{x\}\) the strict localization of \(A[x]\) at the prime ideal generated by \(\operatorname{rad} A\) and \(x\). Let \(U = \operatorname{Spec} A\{x\}[1/x]\). Then for \(n\) prime to the residue characteristic of \(A\), we have \[H^q(U, \mu_n) \simeq \begin{cases} \mu_n(A) & \text{if} \quad q = 0 \\ \mathbb{Z}/n & \text{if} \quad q = 1 \\ 0 & \text{if} \quad q > 1. \end{cases}\]

Indeed, let \(X = \operatorname{Spec} A[x]\), and let \(Y = V(x)\) be the locus of zeros of \(x\) in \(X\). Then \((Y, X)\) is a smooth pair (XVI 3.1) over \(\operatorname{Spec} A\). By (V 4, VIII 5), \(H^q(U, \mu_n)\) is identified with the stalk of the sheaf \(\underline{H}^{q+1}_Y(X, \mu_n)\) at a geometric point over the point \((\operatorname{rad} A, x)\) of \(X\), and the corollary therefore follows immediately from (XVI 3.7). Note that \(\mu_n\) and \(\mathbb{Z}/n\) are both cyclic groups of order \(n\). We have put them here in order to give the canonical formulas (cf. 3.4).

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 1.2

Let \(k\) be a separably closed field, and \(U = \operatorname{Spec} k[[x_1, \ldots, x_r]][1/x_r]\). Then for \(n\) prime to the characteristic of \(k\), we have \[H^q(U, \mu_n) = \begin{cases} \mu_n(A) & \text{if} \quad q = 0 \\ \mathbb{Z}/n & \text{if} \quad q = 1 \\ 0 & \text{if} \quad q > 1. \end{cases}\]

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark

The proof is also valid for the ring of convergent power series, in the case \(k = \mathbb{C}\). Moreover, one easily avoids the hypothesis that \(k\) be separably closed by formulating the statement with a little more care. But in order to establish the general purity theorem 3.2 (under the hypothesis of resolution of singularities, of course), we need the result only in the case \(k\) separably closed, and these other assertions are corollaries of this theorem 3.2.
For dimensions 0, 1, one can prove the result for every regular strictly local ring:

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 1.3

Let \(A\) be a regular strictly local ring and \(x \in \operatorname{rad} A\) a local parameter. Let \(U = \operatorname{Spec} A[1/x]\). Then \(H^0(U, \mu_n) = \mu_n(A)\), and we have canonical isomorphisms \[\mathbb{Z}/n \;\simeq\; H^0(U, \mathbb{G}_m)/(H^0(U, \mathbb{G}_m))^n \;\simeq\; H^1(U, \mu_n),\] where the generator of \(\mathbb{Z}/n\) is the "residue" of \(x \in H^0(U, \mathbb{G}_m)\).

Proof. For \(q = 0\), the assertion is that \(U\) is connected and non-empty. This is true. For \(q = 1\), let us apply the Kummer exact sequence (IX 3.7). We have \(\operatorname{Pic} U = 0\) because \(A\) is regular and factorial, and \(U\) is an open set of \(X = \operatorname{Spec} A\). It follows that we have the exact sequence \[H^0(U, \mathbb{G}_m) \xrightarrow{\ n\ } H^0(U, \mathbb{G}_m) \longrightarrow H^1(U, \mu_n) \longrightarrow 0,\] and it remains to prove that \(H^0(U, \mathbb{G}_m)/(H^0(U, \mathbb{G}_m))^n\) is isomorphic to \(\mathbb{Z}/n\) and generated by the residue of \(x\). Now we have an obvious exact sequence \[\xymatrix@C=2.5em{ 0 \ar[r] & H^0(X, \mathbb{G}_m) \ar[r] \ar@{=}[d] & H^0(U, \mathbb{G}_m) \ar[r] \ar@{=}[d] & \mathbb{Z} \ar[r] & 0 \\ & A^* & A[1/x]^* & & }\] where the image of a section \(a \in H^0(U, \mathbb{G}_m)\) in \(\mathbb{Z}\) is the order of the zero of \(a\) along \(\{x = 0\}\). The group \(A^*\) is divisible by \(n\), because \(A\) is strictly local and \(n\) is prime to the residue characteristic. Indeed, if \(u \in H^0(X, \mathbb{G}_m)\), the equation \(Y^n - u = 0\) defines a finite étale extension of \(A\), which is therefore completely split. It follows that \(H^1(U, \mu_n) \simeq \mathbb{Z}/n\), whence the lemma.

Proof of 1.2. It remains to treat the case \(q > 1\). Let us recall the terminology of (V, appendix). We have \[H^q(U, \mu_n) = \varinjlim_{\mathbb{U}} H^q(\mathbb{U}, \mu_n)\] where \(\mathbb{U} = \left\{ U_0 \mathrel{\substack{\longleftarrow \\ \longleftarrow}} U_1 \mathrel{\substack{\longleftarrow \\ \longleftarrow \\ \longleftarrow}} \cdots \right\}\) runs through the category (filtered, up to homotopy) of hypercoverings of \(U\). Let \(\mathbb{U}\) be such a hypercovering, and take the \(U_i\) separated and of finite type. Since we wish to prove that \(H^q(U, \mu_n) = 0\), it suffices to find a hypercovering \(\mathbb{V}\) and a morphism \(\mathbb{V} \to \mathbb{U}\) such that the induced morphism \[H^q(\mathbb{U}, \mu_n) \longrightarrow H^q(\mathbb{V}, \mu_n)\] is the zero morphism.

Let \(\{W_1, \ldots, W_m\}\) be the set of connected components of all the \(U_i\) for \(i \leqslant q+1\), and let \(B_j\) be the normalization of \(A = k[[x_1, \ldots, x_r]]\) in the field \(R(W_j)\) of rational functions on \(W_j\). Then, since \(W_j \to U\) is étale, the scheme \(W_j\) is an open set of \(\operatorname{Spec} B_j\), say the open set complementary to \(\operatorname{Spec} C_j\), where \(C_j\) is a suitable reduced quotient ring of \(B_j\).

Let us moreover choose an element \(b_j\) of \(B_j\) such that \(b_j\) generates the separable extension \(R(W_j)\) of \(k((x_1, \ldots, x_r))\). Let \(f_j(Y) \in A[Y]\) be the monic irreducible polynomial of \(b_j\) over \(A\), so that \(B_j\) is isomorphic to the normalization of the ring \(A[Y]/(f_j)\). Finally, let \(d_j \in A\) be the discriminant of \(f_j(Y)\), which is a non-zero element of \(A\).
Now it is permissible to replace the \(x_i\) for \(i < r\) by other elements of \(A\), the only condition being that \(\{x_1, \ldots, x_r\}\) must form a system of parameters of \(A\).
It is easy to see that, by changing these elements if necessary, one may assume that the following hypotheses are satisfied:

1. (i) For each \(j\) such that \(d_j\) is not a unit, \(x_1, \ldots, x_{r-1}, d_j\) generate an ideal primary to \(\operatorname{rad} A\).
  2. (ii) For each \(j\), the images of \(x_1, \ldots, x_{r-1}\) in \(C_j\) generate an ideal primary to \(\operatorname{rad} C_j\).
Then we have the following lemma:

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 1.5

Let \(A^0 = k[[x_1, \ldots, x_{r-1}]]\{x_r\}\) be the henselization of \(k[[x_1, \ldots, x_{r-1}]][x_r]\) at the point \((x_1, \ldots, x_r)\), and let \(X^0 = \operatorname{Spec} A^0\) and \(U^0 = \operatorname{Spec} A^0[1/x_r]\). Under conditions 1.4 above, there exists a hypercovering \(\mathbb{U}^0\) of \(U^0\) (of order \(q+1\)) and an isomorphism \(\mathbb{U}^0 \times_{X^0} X \simeq \mathbb{U}\).

Let us grant the lemma. Now the ring \(A^0\) is excellent (EGA IV 7.8.3 (ii), 7.9.5), and consequently the connected components of the \(U^0_i\) and of the \(U_i\) are in one-to-one correspondence (EGA IV 7.8.3 (vii)). The isomorphism \(\mathbb{U}^0 \times_{X^0} X \simeq \mathbb{U}\) therefore gives an isomorphism \[H^q(\mathbb{U}^0, \mu_n) \simeq H^q(\mathbb{U}, \mu_n).\] Since \(k\) is separably closed, \(A^0\) is a strictly local ring, and one can apply 1.1 to the ring \(A^0\). It follows that \(H^q(U^0, \mu_n) = 0\). But \[H^q(U^0, \mu_n) \simeq \varinjlim_{\mathbb{U}^0} H^q(\mathbb{U}^0, \mu_n),\] where \(\mathbb{U}^0\) runs through the category of hypercoverings of \(U^0\) of order \(q+1\), and \(H^q(\mathbb{U}^0, \mu_n)\) is a finite group. Consequently, there exists a morphism of hypercoverings \(\mathbb{V}^0 \to \mathbb{U}^0\) such that the induced morphism \[H^q(\mathbb{U}^0, \mu_n) \longrightarrow H^q(\mathbb{V}^0, \mu_n)\] is the zero morphism. Set \(\mathbb{V} = \mathbb{V}^0 \times_{X^0} X\). Then \(H^q(\mathbb{V}^0, \mu_n) \simeq H^q(\mathbb{V}, \mu_n)\) (same reasoning as for \(\mathbb{U}^0\)), so \[H^q(\mathbb{U}, \mu_n) \longrightarrow H^q(\mathbb{V}, \mu_n)\] is also the zero morphism, q.e.d.

Proof of 1.5. It suffices to find finite \(A^0\)-algebras \(B^0_j\), \(C^0_j\) and \(A\)-isomorphisms \[\begin{aligned} B^0_j \otimes_{A^0} A &\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } B_j \\ C^0_j \otimes_{A^0} A &\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } C_j. \end{aligned}\] Indeed, by ([3] 1.4) the morphism \(B_j \to C_j\) is induced by a morphism \(B^0_j \to C^0_j\), so the open set \(W_j \subset \operatorname{Spec} B_j\) is induced by an open set \(W^0_j \subset \operatorname{Spec} B^0_j\). Moreover, the \(U\)-morphisms between the \(W_j\) are induced by morphisms between the \(A\)-algebras \(B_j\), hence ([3] 1.4) by morphisms between the \(B^0_j\), hence by \(U^0\)-morphisms of the \(W^0_j\). It follows that the \(W^0_j\) form the set of connected components of a simplicial object \(\mathbb{U}^0\) over \(U^0\) that induces \(\mathbb{U}\), and one sees immediately that it is a hypercovering of \(U^0\).

Now 1.4 (ii) indeed implies that \(C_j\) is induced by an \(A^0\)-algebra \(C^0_j\), as one verifies easily (∗). For \(B_j\), it suffices to find a monic polynomial \(f^0_j(Y) \in A^0[Y]\) such that the two \(A\)-algebras \[A[Y]/(f_j) \quad \text{and} \quad A[Y]/(f^0_j) = A \otimes_{A^0} A^0[Y]/(f^0_j)\] are isomorphic. Indeed, \(A^0[Y]/(f^0_j)\) is then reduced, and we take for \(B^0_j\) the normalization (EGA IV 7.8.3 (vi)) of \(A^0[Y]/(f^0_j)\). The ring \(B^0_j \otimes_{A^0} A\) is again normal (EGA IV 7.8.3 (vii)) and birational to \(B_j\), hence equal to this ring.

By 1.4 (i), the ideal \(I_j \subset A\) generated by \(d_j\) is induced by an ideal of \(k[[x_1, \ldots, x_{r-1}]][x_r]\) (Weierstrass preparation theorem [5] [6]), hence by an ideal \(I^0_j\) of \(A^0\). Moreover, \(A/I_j\) is a finite \(k[[x_1, \ldots, x_{r-1}]]\)-algebra, hence is isomorphic to \(A^0/I^0_j\). This last ring is therefore complete, and consequently the \(I^0_j\)-adic completion of \(A^0\) is complete and isomorphic to \(A\). We can therefore find a monic polynomial \(f^0_j \in A^0[Y]\) such that in \(A[Y]\), we have \[f_j \equiv f^0_j \quad (\text{modulo } d_j^2 \operatorname{rad} A).\] By ([3], 1.3), \(A[Y]/(f_j) \simeq A[Y]/(f^0_j)\), whence the lemma.

footnotes.html: (∗) Indeed, 1.4 (ii) implies that \(C_j\) is finite over \(k[[x_1,\ldots,x_{r-1}]]\), and a fortiori over \(A^0\), and it suffices to take \(C^0_j = C_j\) with the \(A^0\)-module structure obtained by restriction of scalars.

pages.title: 2. The case of a strictly local ring.

blocks.html: 2. The case of a strictly local ring.
The theorem is the following:

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 2.1 (∗)

Let \(A\) be an excellent, regular, strictly local ring of equal characteristic, and let \(x\) be a "local parameter" (∗∗) of \(A\). Let \(U = \operatorname{Spec} A[1/x]\). Then for \(n\) prime to the characteristic of \(A\), we have \[H^q(U, \mu_n) = \begin{cases} \mu_n(A) & \text{if} \quad q = 0 \\ \mathbb{Z}/n & \text{if} \quad q = 1 \\ 0 & \text{if} \quad q > 1. \end{cases}\]
The proof is by induction on \(q\). We denote by \(P(N)\) the statement of 2.1 for the values of \(q \leqslant N\). By 1.3, the assertion \(P(1)\) is true.

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 2.2

Suppose that \(P(N)\) is true. Let \(A \to A'\) be a local morphism of excellent, regular, strictly local rings of equal characteristic. Let \(\{x_1, \ldots, x_r\}\) be part of a regular system of parameters of \(A\) whose set of images in \(A'\) is again part of a regular system of parameters. Let \[U = \operatorname{Spec} A[1/x_1, \ldots, 1/x_r]\] \[U' = \operatorname{Spec} A'[1/x'_1, \ldots, 1/x'_r].\] Then the canonical morphism \[H^q(U, \mu_n) \longrightarrow H^q(U', \mu_n)\] is bijective for each \(q \leqslant N\).

Proof. (∗) Induction on \(r\); the assertion is trivial for \(r = 0\). Let \(r > 0\) and suppose the theorem is proved for \(r - 1\). Let \(B = A/(x)\), \(V = \operatorname{Spec} A[1/x_1, \ldots, 1/x_{r-1}]\), \(Y = \operatorname{Spec} B[1/x_1, \ldots, 1/x_{r-1}]\) (where we denote by the same symbol the image of \(x_i\) in \(B\)). There is an open immersion \(i : U \to V\) and \(Y\) is the complementary closed set, defined by the element \(x_r\).

Applying \(P(N)\) to the strict localizations of \(V\) at the geometric points of \(Y\), we find that \[(2.3)\qquad R^q i_*(\mu_n)_U = \begin{cases} (\mu_n)_V & \text{if} \quad q = 0 \\ (\mathbb{Z}/n)_Y & \text{if} \quad q = 1 \\ 0 & \text{if} \quad 1 < q \leqslant N, \end{cases}\] because these strict localizations are excellent regular rings of equal characteristic, and the element \(x_r\) is a local parameter at each point of \(Y\).

Let us denote with a "prime" the analogous objects deduced from \(A'\). We obtain a morphism of spectral sequences \[\xymatrix@C=1em@R=3em{ E_2^{pq} = H^p(V, R^q i_* \mu_n) \ar@{=>}[r] \ar[d]_{\varphi_2^{pq}} & H^{p+q}(U, \mu_n) \ar[d]^{\varphi} \\ E'^{pq}_2 = H^p(V', R^q i'_* \mu_n) \ar@{=>}[r] & H^{p+q}(U', \mu_n). }\] Now it is evident by 1.3 and 2.3 that the base change \(V \xleftarrow{\ g\ } V'\) induces an isomorphism \[g^* R^q i_* \mu_n \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } R^q i'_* \mu_n\] for \(q \leqslant N\) (it is only for \(q = 0,1\) that there is some small thing to verify). Consequently, the induction hypothesis, applied to the morphism \[H^q(V, \mu_n) \longrightarrow H^q(V', \mu_n),\] implies that \(\varphi_2^{pq}\) is an isomorphism for \(q = 0\) and \(p \leqslant N\).

Similarly, one can apply the induction hypothesis to the ring morphism \(B \to B'\) — these are regular, excellent, strictly local rings of equal characteristic, and the elements \(x_1, \ldots, x_{r-1}\) form part of a system of parameters. Hence \[H^q(Y, \mu_n) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } H^q(Y', \mu_n) \quad \text{if} \quad q \leqslant N.\] Since \((\mu_n)_Y \simeq (\mathbb{Z}/n)_Y\), it follows that \(\varphi_2^{pq}\) is also bijective for \(p \leqslant N\) and for \(q = 1\).

From the fact that \(R^q i_* \mu_n = R^q i'_* \mu_n = 0\) if \(1 < q \leqslant N\), we find \(E_2^{pq} = E'^{pq}_2 = 0\) if \(1 < q \leqslant N\), and the morphism of spectral sequences therefore reduces, for \(1 \leqslant m \leqslant N\), to a morphism of exact sequences \[\xymatrix@C=0.9em{ H^{m-2}(Y,\mathbb{Z}/n) \ar[r] \ar[d]^{a} & H^m(V,\mu_n) \ar[r] \ar[d]^{b} & H^m(U,\mu_n) \ar[r]^-{e} \ar[d]^{c} & H^{m-1}(Y,\mathbb{Z}/n) \ar[r] \ar[d]^{d} & H^{m+1}(V,\mu_n) \ar[d] \\ H^{m-2}(Y',\mathbb{Z}/n) \ar[r] & H^m(V',\mu_n) \ar[r] & H^m(U',\mu_n) \ar[r] & H^{m-1}(Y',\mathbb{Z}/n) \ar[r] & H^{m+1}(V',\mu_n). }\] Now we have already seen that \(a\), \(b\), \(d\) are bijective, and it follows that \(c\) is injective. To prove that \(c\) is surjective, it suffices to prove that the morphism \[H^m(U, \mu_n) \xrightarrow{\ e\ } H^{m-1}(Y, \mathbb{Z}/n)\] is surjective for \(m \leqslant N\).

Let \(k \subset A\) be an arbitrary separably closed field, and let \(A^0 = k[x_1, \ldots, x_r]\) be the henselization of \(k[x_1, \ldots, x_r]\) at the origin. Then the hypotheses of 2.1 are satisfied for the morphism \(A^0 \to A\) and for the elements \(x_i\). With the obvious notations, we have a commutative square \[\xymatrix@C=3em{ H^m(U^0,\mu_n) \ar[r]^-{e^0} \ar[d]_{c^0} & H^{m-1}(Y^0, \mathbb{Z}/n) \ar[d]^{d^0} \\ H^m(U,\mu_n) \ar[r]^-{e} & H^{m-1}(Y, \mathbb{Z}/n) }\] and we already know that the arrow \(d^0\) is bijective. It thus suffices to prove that the morphism \(e^0\) is surjective. We are therefore reduced (dropping the \({}^0\)) to verifying surjectivity in the case \(A = k\{x_1, \ldots, x_r\}\).

For this ring, which is a limit of smooth schemes over \(k\), we had proved the purity theorem in XVI 3.7. We thus have \(R^q i_* \mu_n = 0\) for each \(q > 1\), and consequently an exact sequence \[H^m(U, \mu_n) \xrightarrow{\ e\ } H^{m-1}(Y, \mathbb{Z}/n) \longrightarrow H^{m+1}(V, \mu_n) \xrightarrow{\ f\ } H^{m+1}(U, \mu_n)\] for each \(m \geqslant 1\). The surjectivity of \(e\) is therefore equivalent to the injectivity of \(f\).

Let \(Z = \operatorname{Spec} k\{x_1, \ldots, x_{r-1}\}[1/x_1, \ldots, 1/x_{r-1}]\). The morphism \(\operatorname{Spec} k\{x_1, \ldots, x_r\} \to \operatorname{Spec} k\{x_1, \ldots, x_{r-1}\}\) given by the inclusion of rings is acyclic. This is the local acyclicity of a smooth morphism (XVI 1.1). Since the open set \(V\) of \(\operatorname{Spec} k\{x_1, \ldots, x_r\}\) is the inverse image of \(Z\), the morphism \[H^q(Z, \mu_n) \longrightarrow H^q(V, \mu_n)\] is bijective for each \(q\) (XV 1.3). It therefore suffices to prove that the morphism \[H^q(Z, \mu_n) \longrightarrow H^q(U, \mu_n)\] is injective for each \(q\).

Now \(k\{x_1, \ldots, x_r\}\) is an inductive limit of rings \(A_\alpha\) étale over \(k\{x_1, \ldots, x_{r-1}\}[x_r]\), with a lifting of the point \(x_1 = x_2 = \cdots = x_r = 0\) to this ring. Consequently, \(U\) is a projective limit of the open sets \(U_\alpha = \operatorname{Spec} A_\alpha[1/x_1, \ldots, 1/x_r]\), and we have \[H^q(U, \mu_n) = \varinjlim_\alpha H^q(U_\alpha, \mu_n).\] But since \(A_\alpha[1/x_r]\) is smooth over the henselian ring \(k\{x_1, \ldots, x_{r-1}\}\), and the closed fibre of \(A[1/x_r]\) is non-empty, one sees immediately that the \(k\{x_1, \ldots, x_{r-1}\}\)-algebra \(A_\alpha[1/x_r]\) admits sections. Hence \(U_\alpha\) admits sections over \(Z\), and it follows that \[H^q(Z, \mu_n) \longrightarrow H^q(U_\alpha, \mu_n)\] is injective for each \(q\), so that \[H^q(Z, \mu_n) \longrightarrow H^q(U, \mu_n)\] is also injective, whence the lemma.

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 2.4

Suppose that \(P(N)\) is true. Let \(A \to A'\) be a regular morphism (EGA IV 6.8.1) of excellent, strictly local rings of equal characteristic (not necessarily regular), and \(U \subset \operatorname{Spec} A\) an open set which is regular. Let \(U' = U \times_{\operatorname{Spec} A} \operatorname{Spec} A'\). Then for \(n\) prime to the residue characteristic of \(A\), the morphism \[H^q(U, \mu_n) \longrightarrow H^q(U', \mu_n)\] is bijective for \(q \leqslant N\).

Proof. Let \(f : X \to \operatorname{Spec} A\) be a resolution of singularities of \(\operatorname{Spec} A\) such that the open set \(U\) of \(\operatorname{Spec} A\) lifts to an open set \(i : U \to X\), and the closed set \(Y = X - U\) is purely of codimension 1 and with transversal intersections. Let us denote by a \({}'\) the base change induced by \(A \to A'\). The morphism \(g : X' \to X\) is regular (EGA IV 6.8.3), so \(f' : X' \to \operatorname{Spec} A'\) is a resolution of \(\operatorname{Spec} A'\), \(i' : U' \to X'\) an open immersion, and \(Y' = X' - U'\) is purely of codimension 1, with transversal intersections. All these schemes are excellent.

Let \(p'\) be a point of \(X'\) and \(p\) its image in \(X\). Since \(Y\) has transversal intersections in \(X\), there exist elements \(x_1, \ldots, x_r \in \mathcal{O}_{X,p}\) such that \(\{x_1, \ldots, x_r\}\) is part of a system of parameters of \(\mathcal{O}_{X,p}\) and \(\operatorname{Spec} \mathcal{O}_{X,p} \cap Y = V(x_1, \ldots, x_r)\). Moreover, it follows immediately from the fact that \(g : X' \to X\) is regular that the images \(x'_i\) of the \(x_i\) in \(\mathcal{O}_{X',p'}\) form part of a system of parameters of this ring, and that \(\operatorname{Spec} \mathcal{O}_{X',p'} \cap Y = V(x'_1, \ldots, x'_r)\).

Let \(B'\) be the strict localization of \(\mathcal{O}_{X',p'}\) at a geometric point \(\bar{p}\) over \(p'\), and let \(B\) be the strict localization of \(\mathcal{O}_{X,p}\) at the corresponding geometric point of \(X\) (these are excellent rings (EGA IV 7.8.3 (ii), 7.9.5)). Let \[U_{\bar{p}} = \operatorname{Spec} B[1/x_1, \ldots, 1/x_r], \qquad U'_{\bar{p}} = \operatorname{Spec} B'[1/x'_1, \ldots, 1/x'_r].\] Lemma 2.2 is applicable, and we deduce that the morphisms \[(*)\qquad H^q(U_{\bar{p}}, \mu_n) \longrightarrow H^q(U'_{\bar{p}}, \mu_n)\] are bijective for \(q \leqslant N\).

Let us compute the sheaves \(R^q i_* \mu_n\), \(R^q i'_* \mu_n\) for the open immersions \(i : U \to X\) and \(i' : U' \to X'\): the stalk \((R^q i'_* \mu_n)_{\bar{p}}\) at the geometric point \(\bar{p}\) is none other than \(H^q(U'_{\bar{p}}, \mu_n)\) (VIII 5). Similarly, \((R^q i_* \mu_n)_{\bar{p}} = H^q(U_{\bar{p}}, \mu_n)\). Hence \((*)\) implies that the base change morphisms \[(**)\qquad g^* R^q i_* \mu_n \longrightarrow R^q i'_* \mu_n\] are bijective for \(q \leqslant N\).

By the base change theorem for a proper morphism (XII 5.5), we have (since \(X\) and \(X'\) are proper over the spectra of strictly local rings, and the closed fibres of \(X\) and \(X'\) are equal) \[H^q(X, F) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } H^q(X', g^* F)\] for any torsion sheaf \(F\), for each \(q\). Consequently, \((**)\) implies that in the morphism of spectral sequences \[\xymatrix@C=1em@R=3em{ E_2^{pq} = H^p(X, R^q i_* \mu_n) \ar@{=>}[r] \ar[d]_{\varphi_2^{pq}} & H^{p+q}(U, \mu_n) \ar[d]^{\varphi} \\ E'^{pq}_2 = H^p(X', R^q i'_* \mu_n) \ar@{=>}[r] & H^{p+q}(U', \mu_n), }\] the arrows \(\varphi_2^{pq}\) are bijective for each \(q \leqslant N\). One easily sees that this implies that \(\varphi_\infty^{pq}\) is bijective if \(q \leqslant N\) and \(p+q \leqslant N+1\). Consequently, the morphism of abutments \[H^m(U, \mu_n) \longrightarrow H^m(U', \mu_n)\] is bijective for \(m \leqslant N\), whence the lemma.
The following lemma will complete the proof of 2.1:

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 2.5

\(P(N) \Longrightarrow P(N+1)\).

Proof. Let \(A\) be strictly local, regular, excellent, of equal characteristic, \(x \in \operatorname{rad} A\) a local parameter, \(U = \operatorname{Spec} A[1/x]\). Let \(\hat{A}\) be the completion of \(A\), \(\hat{x}\) the image element of \(x\), \(\hat{U} = \operatorname{Spec} \hat{A}[1/x]\), and \(g : \hat{U} \to U\) the canonical morphism. It suffices to prove that we have \[(2.6)\qquad \begin{aligned} g_*(\mu_n)_{\hat{U}} &\simeq (\mu_n)_U \quad \text{and} \\ R^q g_* \mu_n &= 0 \quad \text{if} \quad 1 \leqslant q \leqslant N. \end{aligned}\] Indeed, the Leray spectral sequence \[E_2^{pq} = H^p(U, R^q g_* \mu_n) \Longrightarrow H^{p+q}(\hat{U}, \mu_n)\] will give isomorphisms \[H^q(U, \mu_n) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } H^q(\hat{U}, \mu_n)\] for \(q \leqslant N\), and an exact sequence \[0 \longrightarrow H^{N+1}(U, \mu_n) \longrightarrow H^{N+1}(\hat{U}, \mu_n) \longrightarrow H^0(U, R^{N+1} g_* \mu_n).\] But we already know that \(P(1)\) is true (1.3), and it is therefore a matter of proving that \(H^q(\hat{U}, \mu_n) = 0\) if \(1 < q \leqslant N+1\). We may thus replace \(A\) by \(\hat{A}\), which is isomorphic to a ring of formal power series \(\hat{A} \simeq k[[x_1, \ldots, x_r]]\) with \(k\) separably closed and \(\hat{x} = x_r\). We treated this case in 1.2.

Let us therefore verify (2.6): the fact that \(g_*(\mu_n)_{\hat{U}} \simeq (\mu_n)_U\) is nothing but the assertion of (2.3) for \(q = 0\). Let us recall that \(R^q g_* \mu_n\) is the sheaf associated to the presheaf \(\mathcal{Q}^q\), where \[\mathcal{Q}^q(V) = H^q(\hat{V}, \mu_n)\] for \(V \to U\) étale. It suffices to take \(V\) separated and of finite type; then \(V\) is a sum of integral schemes, and it suffices to consider such \(V\). Let \(B\) be the normalization of \(A\) in the field of fractions of \(\Gamma(V, \mathcal{O}_V)\). Then \(B\) is a finite \(A\)-algebra (EGA IV 7.8.3 (vi)) and one sees immediately that \(V\) is a regular open set of \(\operatorname{Spec} B\) and that \(\hat{V}\) is the corresponding open set of \(\operatorname{Spec} \hat{B}\), where \(\hat{B} = B \otimes_A \hat{A}\). It follows that the hypotheses of 2.4 are satisfied for the open set \(V \subset \operatorname{Spec} B\), and for the morphism \(B \to \hat{B}\). We thus have \[\mathcal{Q}^q(V) \simeq H^q(V, \mu_n) \simeq H^q(\hat{V}, \mu_n)\] for \(q \leqslant N\). Now the sheaf associated to the presheaf \(V \mapsto H^q(V, \mu_n)\) is obviously zero, whence the lemma.

(∗∗) By which we mean here: an element belonging to a regular system of parameters.

(∗) A shorter proof than the one that follows, but using the formalism of the cup-product, would consist in showing that under the hypothesis \(P(N)\), the cohomology \(H^*(U,\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})\) is, in dimension \(\leqslant N\), the exterior algebra (over \(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}\)) of \(H^1(U,\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}) \simeq (\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^r\), which reduces to establishing 2.2 for \(q = 1\), a well-known case. The computation indicated under the hypothesis \(P(N)\) is worked out for example in SGA 7.

blocks.html: 3. Purity.
We shall adopt a terminology analogous to that of XVI 3:

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 3.1

We call a regular pair \((Y, X)\) of codimension \(c\) a closed immersion \(i : Y \to X\) of locally noetherian regular schemes such that for each \(y \in Y\) one has \(\operatorname{codim}_y(Y, X) = c\) (there then exists an open neighbourhood \(X'\) of \(y\) in \(X\) and sections \(x_1, \ldots, x_c \in \Gamma(X', \mathcal{O}_X)\) which generate the ideal of \(Y\), and which form part of a regular system of parameters of \(X\) at each point of \(Y \cap X'\)). We write \(U = X - Y\), and \(j : U \to X\) the corresponding open immersion.

A morphism \((Y', X') \to (Y, X)\) of regular pairs of codimension \(c\) is a morphism \(X' \to X\) such that \(Y' = Y \times_X X'\). One defines in an obvious analogous manner the notion of regular triple, of morphism of regular triples, etc ...

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 3.2 (∗)

(Cohomological purity) Let \((Y, X)\) be a regular pair of codimension \(c > 0\), where \(X\) is an excellent prescheme of equal characteristic. Let \(F\) be a sheaf on \(X\), locally constant, of cyclic groups of order \(n\) prime to the characteristic of \(X\). Then we have, in the notation of (V 4, VIII 5) \[\underline{H}^q_Y(X, F) = (R^q i^!)F = 0 \quad \text{if} \quad q \neq 2c,\] \[(R^q j_*)j^* F = 0 \quad \text{if} \quad q \neq 0, 2c-1, \quad \text{and}\] \[\underline{H}^{2c}_Y(X, F) = i^*(R^{2c-1} j_*)j^* F\] is a locally constant sheaf of cyclic groups of order \(n\) on \(Y\).

Proof. (cf. XVI 3.7). One sees immediately that we have \[\underline{H}^q_Y(X, F) = 0 \quad \text{if} \quad q = 0,1.\] By (V 4.5) \[\underline{H}^q_Y(X, F) = (R^q i^!)F \simeq i^*(R^{q-1} j_*)j^* F \quad \text{if} \quad q > 1,\] so the assertions for the three sheaves are equivalent. Since the assertions are local on \(X\) for the étale topology, we may assume that \(F = \mu_n\).

For the case \(c = 1\), the computation of the stalks (VIII 5) of \((R^q j_*)j^* \mu_n\) brings us back to the situation considered in 2.1, whence \[((R^q j_*)j^* \mu_n)_{\bar{y}} = \begin{cases} \mathbb{Z}/n & \text{if} \quad q = 1 \\ 0 & \text{if} \quad q > 1 \end{cases}\] for each geometric point \(\bar{y}\) of \(Y\). Since these sheaves are zero outside \(Y\) in any case, this proves the assertion for \(q > 1\). For \(q = 1\) (\(= 2c-1\)), one applies the criterion of (IX 2.13 (i)) and the explicit computation of 1.3.

The case \(c > 1\) is treated by induction (cf. XVI 3.7): Let \((Y, X)\) be a regular pair of codimension \(c > 1\). By the definition, it is clear that, locally on \(X\), one can find a regular triple \((Y, Z, X)\) where \((Z, X)\) is of codimension 1 and \((Y, Z)\) is of codimension \(c-1\). Let \[\xymatrix@R=2.2em@C=1.2em{ Y \ar[rr]^{u} \ar[dr]_{i} & & Z \ar[dl]^{v} \\ & X & }\] be the closed immersions. We have the spectral sequence \[E_2^{pq} = (R^p u^!)(R^q v^!)F \Longrightarrow (R^{p+q} i^!)F.\] By the induction hypothesis, \((R^q v^!)F = 0\) if \(q \neq 2\), and is locally constant etc ... if \(q = 2\). Hence, again by the induction hypothesis, applied to the morphism \(u\), \((R^p u^!)(R^q v^!)F = 0\) if \((p,q) \neq (2c-2, 2)\), and is loc. const. etc ... if \((p,q) = (2c-2, 2)\), whence the result for the abutment \((R^{p+q} i^!)F\), q.e.d.

3.3. It now remains to determine the locally constant sheaves of (3.2) up to canonical isomorphism. For each prescheme \(S\) we introduce the locally constant sheaves \[(\mu_n^{\otimes r})_S = \text{the } r\text{-th tensor product of the sheaf } (\mu_n)_S\] over the constant sheaf of rings \(\mathbb{Z}_S\). Let us also set \((\mu_n^{\otimes 0})_S = (\mathbb{Z}/n)_S\). One notes immediately that if \(n\) is invertible on \(S\), then \((\mu_n^{\otimes r})_S\) is a locally constant sheaf of cyclic groups of order \(n\). We have formulas of the type \[(\mu_n^{\otimes r}) \otimes (\mu_n^{\otimes s}) = (\mu_n^{\otimes r+s}),\] and if \(S' \to S\), then \((\mu_n^{\otimes r})_{S'}\) is canonically isomorphic to the inverse image on \(S'\) of \((\mu_n^{\otimes r})_S\). We shall often omit the symbol \(S\) if there is no confusion to fear.

Let \((Y, X)\) be a regular pair of codimension 1, and suppose that \(Y\) is defined by an equation \(x = 0\). We have the exact sequence of sheaves \[0 \longrightarrow (\mathbb{G}_m)_X \longrightarrow j_*(\mathbb{G}_m)_U \longrightarrow \mathbb{Z}_Y \longrightarrow 0,\] whence, by applying (1.3), canonical isomorphisms \[(3.3.1)\qquad (R^1 j_* \mu_n) \simeq j_*(\mathbb{G}_m)_U/(j_*(\mathbb{G}_m)_U)^n \simeq (\mathbb{Z}/n)_Y,\] which obviously do not depend on the choice of \(x\). Consequently, we have a canonical isomorphism \[(3.3.2)\qquad \varphi : \mathbb{Z}/n \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } (R^2 i^!)\mu_n \simeq i^*(R^1 j_*)\mu_n.\]

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 3.4 (∗)

Let \(\mathcal{C}\) be the family of regular pairs of excellent schemes of equal characteristic. There exists one and only one function \(\varphi\) giving, for each regular pair \((Y, X)\) of codimension \(c\), an isomorphism (called canonical) of sheaves \[\varphi(Y, X) = \varphi : \mathbb{Z}/n \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \underline{H}^{2c}_Y(X, \mu_n^{\otimes c}) = (R^{2c} i^!)\mu_n^{\otimes c}\] such that \(\varphi\) satisfies the following conditions:

(i) If \(c = 1\), and if \(Y\) is defined in \(X\) by an equation \(x = 0\), then \(\varphi\) is the morphism (3.3).

(ii) \(\varphi\) is compatible with morphisms of smooth pairs, that is, if \((Y', X') \to (Y, X)\) is a morphism, let \(g : Y' \to Y\) be the induced morphism. The diagram of \(Y'\)-sheaves \[\xymatrix@C=4em@R=3em{ \mathbb{Z}/n \ar[r]^-{\varphi(Y',X')} \ar[d] & (R^{2c} i^!)\mu_n^{\otimes c} \ar[d] \\ g^*(\mathbb{Z}/n) \ar[r]^-{g^* \varphi(Y,X)} & g^*(R^{2c} i^!)\mu_n^{\otimes c} }\] is commutative (which implies in particular that the right-hand vertical arrow is an isomorphism).

(iii) Transitivity: let \((Z, Y, X)\) be a regular triple, that is, a commutative diagram of closed immersions of regular preschemes etc ..., \[\xymatrix@R=2.2em@C=1.2em{ Z \ar[rr]^{v} \ar[dr]_{w} & & Y \ar[dl]^{u} \\ & X & }\] Let \(a, b, c\) be the codimensions of \(u, v, w\) respectively (so \(c = a+b\)). We have an isomorphism \[\varphi(Y, X) \otimes \mu_n^{\otimes b} : \mu_n^{\otimes b} \longrightarrow (R^{2a} u^!)\mu_n^{\otimes a} \otimes \mu_n^{\otimes b} \simeq (R^{2a} u^!)\mu_n^{\otimes c}.\] The spectral sequence \((R^p v^!)(R^q u^!)F \Longrightarrow (R^{p+q} w^!)F\) gives an isomorphism \[\xi : (R^{2b} v^!)(R^{2a} u^!)\mu_n^{\otimes c} \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } (R^{2c} w^!)\mu_n^{\otimes c}.\] We thus obtain a diagram of isomorphisms \[(3.4.1)\qquad \xymatrix@C=4em@R=3.2em{ \mathbb{Z}/n \ar[r]^-{\varphi(Z,Y)} \ar[d]_{\varphi(Z,X)} & (R^{2b} v^!)\mu_n^{\otimes b} \ar[d]^{\eta} \\ (R^{2c} w^!)\mu_n^{\otimes c} & (R^{2b} v^!)(R^{2a} u^!)\mu_n^{\otimes c} \ar[l]^-{\xi} }\] where \(\eta = (R^{2b} v^!)(\varphi(Y,X) \otimes \mu_n^{\otimes b})\), and the transitivity assertion is that this diagram is commutative.

Proof. The proof of existence and uniqueness is by induction on the codimension \(c\). For \(c = 1\), one defines the morphism \(\varphi\) locally with (3.3.1). Since this morphism does not depend on the choice of the parameter \(x\), one obtains an isomorphism \(\varphi\) for each \((Y, X)\) of codimension 1 by gluing, and it is clear, from the definition of the morphism and from 1.3, that the \(\varphi\) thus constructed satisfies (ii). Transitivity does not come into play for \(c = 1\).

Suppose now that existence and uniqueness are already proved if the codimension is \(< c\), and that \(c > 1\). Applying the induction hypothesis, one notes immediately that in the situation of 3.4 (iii) the three arrows of 3.4.1 which are already defined, i.e. \(\varphi(Z,Y)\), \(\xi\), \(\eta\), are compatible with morphisms of regular triples. In this situation, set \[\Psi(Z,Y,X) = \xi\, \eta\, \varphi(Z,Y),\] so \(\Psi\) is also compatible with morphisms of triples. Now if \((Z,X)\) is a regular pair of codimension \(c > 1\), one can, locally on \(X\), find a triple \((Z,Y,X)\) with \(0 < \operatorname{codim}(Y,X) < c\). Everything therefore comes down to proving that the arrow \(\Psi(Z,Y,X)\) is independent of \(Y\). Indeed, this will prove the uniqueness of \(\varphi\) for codimension \(c\), and existence will follow by gluing.

If \((Z,Y,X)\) is arbitrary such that \(\operatorname{codim}(Y,X) > 1\), one can, locally on \(X\), find a regular triple \((Y,W,X)\) where the codimension of \((W,X)\) is equal to 1. By a transitivity diagram chase, which we leave to the reader, one is thus reduced to verifying the independence of \(Y\) when \((Y,X)\) is of codimension 1.

Let \((Z,Y_0,X)\) and \((Z,Y_1,X)\) be two such triples. It suffices to carry out the verification fibre by fibre, and one is thus reduced to the case \(X\) strictly local, and \(Y_i\) defined by an equation, say \(f_i = 0\) (\(i=0,1\)). Let \(\bar{X} = \operatorname{Spec} \mathcal{O}_X[t]\), \(\bar{Z} = Z \times_X \bar{X}\), and \(\bar{Y}\) the closed subscheme of \(\bar{X}\) defined by the equation \[(f_1 - f_0)t + f_0 = 0.\] Then \(\bar{Y}\) is obviously regular at the points over the sections \(\varepsilon_0 : \{t=0\}\) and \(\varepsilon_1 : \{t=1\}\) of \(\bar{X}/X\). Let \(C\) be the closed subset (EGA IV 7.8.3 (iv)) of \(\bar{Y}\) of the points where \(\bar{Y}\) is not regular, and let us replace \(\bar{X}, \bar{Y}, \bar{Z}\) by \(\bar{X} - C\), \(\bar{Y} - C\), \(\bar{Z} - C \cap \bar{Z}\) respectively. Then \((\bar{Z}, \bar{Y}, \bar{X})\) is a regular triple, and the sections \(\varepsilon_i\) give morphisms of triples \[(Z, Y_i, X) \longrightarrow (\bar{Z}, \bar{Y}, \bar{X}) \quad (i=0,1).\]

Let \(F = (R^{2c} w^!)\mu_n^{\otimes c}\) be the sheaf on \(Z\). It is a locally constant sheaf, isomorphic to \(\mathbb{Z}/n\) (by either of the isomorphisms \(\Psi(Z, Y_i, X)\)), and one notes immediately that the sheaf \(\bar{F} = (R^{2c} \bar{w}^!)\mu_n^{\otimes c}\) on \(\bar{Z}\) is the inverse image on \(\bar{Z}\) of \(F\). Since the fibres of \(\bar{Z} \to Z\) are connected and non-empty and \(\bar{Z} \to Z\) is smooth, hence open, it follows that the induced morphism \[H^0(Z, F) \longrightarrow H^0(\bar{Z}, \bar{F})\] is bijective, so that each of the morphisms \[(*)\qquad \xymatrix@R=1.4em@C=3em{ & & H^0(Z, F) \\ H^0(Z, F) \ar[r] & H^0(\bar{Z}, \bar{F}) \ar[ur]^{\varepsilon_0^*} \ar[dr]_{\varepsilon_1^*} & \\ & & H^0(Z, F) }\] is bijective, so that \(\varepsilon_0^* = \varepsilon_1^*\).

Now to give an isomorphism of a sheaf \(F\) with \(\mathbb{Z}/n\) amounts to giving a global section (the image of 1) which is a generator. Let \(\bar{\alpha}\), \(a_i\) be the global sections of \(\bar{F}\), \(F\) given by the isomorphisms \(\Psi(\bar{Z}, \bar{Y}, \bar{X})\), \(\Psi(Z, Y_i, X)\) respectively. Since \(\Psi(.,.,.)\) is compatible with the morphisms, the diagram \((*)\) implies that \[a_0 = \varepsilon_0^*(\bar{\alpha}) = \varepsilon_1^*(\bar{\alpha}) = a_1,\] whence \(\Psi(Z, Y_0, X) = \Psi(Z, Y_1, X)\), q.e.d.

This theorem may also be regarded as the conjunction of 3.2 and the variance theory of Exp XVIII through the "local fundamental classes", where one studies homomorphisms \(\varphi(Y,X)\) (not necessarily bijective) for \(Y\) locally a complete intersection in \(X\).

pages.title: 4. Local acyclicity of a regular morphism.

blocks.html: 4. Local acyclicity of a regular morphism.

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 4.1 (∗)

(local acyclicity). Let \(g : X' \to X\) be a regular morphism (EGA IV 6.8.1) of excellent schemes of equal characteristic. Then \(g\) is universally locally acyclic for \(n\) prime to the characteristic.

Proof. Since the hypothesis is stable under base change of finite type, it follows at once from XV 1.13 ii) that it suffices to prove that \(g\) is locally acyclic for \(n\). Let us apply the criterion of XV 1.17: Let \(\bar{x}'\) be a geometric point of \(X'\) and \(\bar{x}\) the corresponding geometric point of \(X\). It follows immediately from the definition of regular morphism that the morphism of strict localizations at these points induced by \(g\) is again regular. We are therefore reduced to the case where \(X = \operatorname{Spec} A\) and \(X' = \operatorname{Spec} A'\) are strictly local, \(g\) is a local morphism, and by XV 1.17 it suffices to prove that the geometric fibres of \(g\) are acyclic for \(n\). Replacing \(X\) by an integral closed subscheme and \(X'\) by the corresponding closed set, we are reduced to the case of the generic geometric fibre \(X'_{\bar{x}}\). Let us take \(\bar{x} = \operatorname{Spec} \bar{K}\) where \(\bar{K}\) is the separable closure of the field of rational functions on \(X\). Then we have \[\bar{x} = \varprojlim_\alpha U_\alpha\] where \(U_\alpha\) runs through a filtered category of connected étale \(X\)-schemes, which we may assume to be regular (EGA IV 7.8.3 (v)). Let \(B_\alpha\) be the normalization of \(A\) in the field of rational functions \(R(U_\alpha)\). Set \(U'_\alpha = X' \times_X U_\alpha\) and \(B'_\alpha = A' \otimes_A B_\alpha\). Then \(U_\alpha\) is a regular open set of \(\operatorname{Spec} B_\alpha\) and \(B_\alpha \to B'_\alpha\) is regular, hence by 2.4 \[H^q(U_\alpha, \mu_n) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } H^q(U'_\alpha, \mu_n)\] for each \(q\). Now the fibre \(X'_{\bar{x}}\) is the limit of the \(U'_\alpha\), so \[\begin{aligned} H^q(X'_{\bar{x}}, \mu_n) &= \varinjlim_\alpha H^q(U'_\alpha, \mu_n) \\ &= \varinjlim_\alpha H^q(U_\alpha, \mu_n) \\ &= H^q(\bar{x}, \mu_n) = 0 \quad \text{if} \quad q > 0, \quad \text{q.e.d.} \end{aligned}\]

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 4.2

(base change by a regular morphism). Let \[\xymatrix@C=3em@R=3em{ X \ar[d]_{f} & X' \ar[l]_{g} \ar[d]^{f'} \\ Y & Y' \ar[l]^{g} }\] be a cartesian diagram, \(g : Y' \to Y\) being a regular morphism of excellent preschemes of equal characteristic, \(f\) quasi-compact and quasi-separated. Then for each abelian torsion sheaf \(F\) prime to the characteristic, the base change morphisms (XII 4.2) \[g^*(R^q f_*)F \longrightarrow (R^q f'_*)g'^* F\] are bijective for each \(q \geqslant 0\).
This follows from 4.1 and XVI 1.1.
From 4.1 and XV 1.17 one deduces immediately

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 4.3

Let \(A\) be an excellent strictly local ring of equal characteristic, and \(f : X \to \operatorname{Spec} A\) a morphism. Let \(A \to A'\) be a regular morphism, where \(A'\) is also strictly local, excellent, of equal characteristic. Let us denote by a \({}'\) the base change induced by \(A \to A'\). For each torsion sheaf \(F\) on \(X\), prime to the characteristic of \(A\), we have \[H^q(X, F) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } H^q(X', F')\] for each \(q \geqslant 0\).

This corollary applies in particular in the case where \(A'\) is the completion \(\hat{A}\) of \(A\). (In this case, one can moreover replace the hypothesis "\(A\) strictly local" by "\(A\) local henselian", as one notes immediately.)

blocks.html: 5. Finiteness theorem.

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 5.1 (∗)

(finiteness). Let \(f : X \to S\) be a morphism of finite type of excellent schemes of equal characteristic, and let \(F\) be an abelian torsion sheaf prime to the characteristic on \(X\), which is a constructible sheaf. Then the \((R^q f_*)F\) are also constructible for each \(q\).
This result generalizes the theorem of XVI 5.1. The proof is roughly the same: one applies the purity result 3.2 instead of XVI 3.7.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 5.2

Let \(A\) be an excellent strictly local ring of equal characteristic and \(f : X \to \operatorname{Spec} A\) a morphism of finite type. Let \(F\) be an abelian sheaf on \(X\), torsion prime to the characteristic of \(A\), and constructible. Then the \(H^q(X, F)\) are finite groups for each \(q\).

footnotes.html: (∗) Depends on the resolution of singularities (cf. Introduction).

blocks.html: 6. Cohomological dimension of affine morphisms.

Let \(f : X \to Y\) be a morphism of finite type of excellent preschemes, and \(F\) a sheaf on \(X\). Let us recall that one has defined (XIV 2.2) an integer \(\delta(F)\) in the case where \(Y\) is local. One can therefore regard \(\delta\) as a function \(\delta(F,f)\) on an arbitrary \(Y\), by setting \[(6.0)\qquad \delta(F,f,y) = \delta(F'),\] where \(Y' = \operatorname{Spec} \mathcal{O}_{Y,y}\), \(X' \to Y'\) is the morphism deduced from \(f\) by the base change \(Y' \to Y\), and \(F'\) is the inverse image sheaf of \(F\) on \(X'\).
We have the following result, which generalizes XIV 3.1:

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 6.1 (∗)

Let \(f : X \to Y\) be an affine morphism of finite type, where \(Y\) is an excellent scheme of equal characteristic, and let \(F\) be an abelian torsion sheaf on \(X\). Then \(R^q f_* F\) is zero at each point \(y \in Y\) such that \(\delta(F,f,y) < q\).
The local variant, obviously equivalent to 6.1, is the following:

blocks.label: 6.1 bis
blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 6.1 bis (∗)

Let \(A\) be an excellent strictly local ring of equal characteristic, and \(f : X \to Y = \operatorname{Spec} A\) an affine morphism of finite type. Let \(F\) be a torsion sheaf on \(X\). Then \[H^q(X, F) = 0 \quad \text{if} \quad q > \delta(F).\]

Let us recall (X 5.1) that there is no interest in such assertions for the \(F\) of \(p\)-torsion, where \(p\) is equal to the characteristic. One can therefore assume \(F\) prime to the characteristic.
We have the following corollary:

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 6.2

Let \(A\) be a henselian, excellent ring of equal characteristic, with residue field \(k\), and let \(U \subset \operatorname{Spec} A\) be an affine open set. Let \(\ell \in \mathbb{P}\). We have \[\operatorname{cd}_\ell U \leqslant \operatorname{cd}_\ell k + \dim A.\]

Indeed, let \(\tilde{A}\) be the strict localization of \(A\), which is an infinite Galois étale covering, of group \(G = G(\bar{k}/k)\), and let \(\tilde{U}\) be the affine open set of \(\operatorname{Spec} \tilde{A}\) induced from \(U\). Applying the Hochschild-Serre spectral sequence (VIII 8.4) \[H^p(G, H^q(\tilde{U}, .)) \Longrightarrow H^{p+q}(U, .)\] we are reduced to treating the case \(A = \tilde{A}\), and then it is a special case of 6.1 bis.

With the notations above, let \(R(A)\) be the ring of rational functions on \(A\). We have \(\operatorname{Spec} R(A) = \varprojlim_\alpha U_\alpha\) where \(U_\alpha\) is an affine open set of \(\operatorname{Spec} A\). It therefore follows from the theory of passage to the limit that we have

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 6.3

Let \(A\) be henselian, excellent, of equal characteristic, with residue field \(k\). Let \(R(A)\) be the field of rational functions on \(\operatorname{Spec} A\). Then for \(\ell \in \mathbb{P}\), we have \[\operatorname{cd}_\ell R(A) \leqslant \operatorname{cd}_\ell k + \dim A\]
with equality if \(\ell\) is invertible in \(k\), and if moreover \(\ell \neq 2\) or \(k\) is not orderable.
The equality in the last case follows from X 2.4.
Finally, applying X 4.2, 4.4, we find

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 6.4

Let \(X\) be an excellent noetherian scheme of equal characteristic, and \(R(X)\) the ring of rational functions on \(X\). Let \(\ell \in \mathbb{P}\) be invertible on \(X\), and suppose that \(\ell \neq 2\) or that no residue field of \(X\) is orderable. Then \[\operatorname{cd}_\ell(X) \leqslant \operatorname{cd}_\ell R(X) + \dim X \leqslant 2 \operatorname{cd}_\ell R(X).\]

Proof of 6.1. We begin with a reduction analogous to that of XIV 3. Induction on \(\delta\): It is clear that 6.1 for \(\delta \leqslant d\) is equivalent to (6.1 bis) for \(\delta \leqslant d\). For \(\delta = 0\), it is trivial. Let us treat the case \(\delta \leqslant 1\), in the form 6.1 bis. Since \(F\) is a limit of its constructible subsheaves (IX 2.9 (iii)), one may assume \(F\) constructible, and then the support of \(F\) is contained in a closed set \(Z \subset X\) with \(\delta(z) \leqslant 1\) for each \(z \in Z\) (XIV 2.2). Each reduced irreducible component \(Z_i\) of \(Z\) is then either an affine scheme of finite type of dimension \(\leqslant 1\) over the closed point \(y\) of \(Y\), or a quasi-finite scheme over a reduced closed subscheme \(C\) of \(Y\) of dimension 1. In this last case, we have \(C = \operatorname{Spec} B\) where \(B\) is an integral strictly local ring of dimension 1. Such a scheme \(Z_i\) is the spectrum of an integral strictly local ring, of dimension \(\leqslant 1\), or of a finite extension of the field of fractions of \(B\). Hence the cohomological dimension of \(Z_i\) is at most equal to 1 in any case, by X 2.3 and IX 5.7. We have an exact sequence \[0 \longrightarrow F \longrightarrow \prod_i F_i \longrightarrow \varepsilon \longrightarrow 0\] where \(F_i\) is the restriction of \(F\) to \(Z_i\), from which we draw the result for \(Z\).
Suppose now that the theorem is proved for the values of \(\delta < d\), and let us prove it for \(\delta(F) \leqslant d\), assuming \(d \geqslant 2\).

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 6.5

It suffices to treat the case where \(X = \mathbb{E}^1_Y = \operatorname{Spec} \mathcal{O}_Y[t]\) is the affine space of dimension 1, and where \(Y\) is strictly local.

The proof is that of XIV 4.2: It is clear that one may assume \(Y\) strictly local, and that \(\delta(F) \leqslant d\). It must be proved that \(H^q(X,F) = 0\) if \(q > d\). One can embed \(X\) in \(\mathbb{E}^N_Y\), so it suffices to treat the case \(X = \mathbb{E}^N_Y\). Induction on \(N\): Let us consider the diagram \[\xymatrix@R=2.2em@C=1.2em{ \mathbb{E}^N_Y \ar[rr]^{g} \ar[dr]_{f} & & \mathbb{E}^{N-1}_Y \ar[dl]^{h} \\ & Y & }\] so that \(\mathbb{E}^N_Y\) is the affine space of dimension 1 over \(\mathbb{E}^{N-1}_Y\). Applying the induction hypothesis and the Leray spectral sequence \[H^p(\mathbb{E}^{N-1}_Y, R^q g_* F) \Longrightarrow H^{p+q}(\mathbb{E}^N_Y, F)\] we see that it suffices to prove that \[\delta(R^q g_* F) \leqslant d-q.\] This means that if \(z \in \mathbb{E}^{N-1}_Y\) is a point such that \(\delta(z) > d-q\), then \(R^q g_* F = 0\) at the point \(z\). But the induction hypothesis on \(N\) applies to the morphism \(g\), and we thus have \(R^q g_* F = 0\) at the point \(z\) if \(\delta(F,g,z) < q\). It thus suffices to prove the inequality \[\delta(F,g,z) + \delta(z) \leqslant \delta(F).\] We leave this pleasure to the reader.

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 6.6

To prove 6.1 for the values of \(\delta \leqslant d\), it suffices to prove the following: Let \(B\) be a complete normal local ring of equal characteristic and of dimension \(d\). Let \(U \subset \operatorname{Spec} B\) be an affine open set. Suppose that there exists an element \(x \in \operatorname{rad} B\) which is invertible on \(U\). Then \[H^q(U, \mathbb{Z}/\ell) = 0 \quad \text{if} \quad q > d.\]
This lemma is moreover a special case of corollary 6.2.

Proof. (cf. XIV 4.4). By 6.5, it suffices to treat the case where \(Y\) is strictly local and \(X = \mathbb{E}^1_Y\). Consider the diagram \[\xymatrix@R=2.2em@C=1.2em{ \mathbb{E}^1_Y \ar[rr]^{i} \ar[dr]_{f} & & \mathbb{P}^1_Y \ar[dl]^{g} \\ & Y & }\] where \(\mathbb{P}^1_Y\) is the projective space and \(\mathbb{E}^1_Y\) is obtained from \(\mathbb{P}^1\) by removing the section \(Y_\infty\) at infinity. Let \(F\) be a torsion sheaf on \(\mathbb{E}^1\), with \(\delta(F) \leqslant d\). We have the spectral sequence \[H^p(\mathbb{P}^1, R^q i_* F) \Longrightarrow H^{p+q}(\mathbb{E}^1, F).\] Now the \(R^q i_* F\) for \(q > 0\) are concentrated on the section \(Y_\infty\), which is isomorphic to \(Y\). Since \(Y\) is strictly local, it follows that \(H^p(\mathbb{P}^1, R^q i_* F) = 0\) if \(p > 0\) and \(q > 0\). Moreover, by XII 5.3, we have \(H^p(\mathbb{P}^1, i_* F) = 0\) if \(p > 2\). Since we want to prove that \(H^n(\mathbb{E}^1, F) = 0\) if \(n > d\), and since \(d \geqslant 2\), it suffices to prove that \[H^0(\mathbb{P}^1, R^q i_* F) = H^0(Y_\infty, R^q i_* F) = 0 \quad \text{if} \quad q > d.\] This group is isomorphic to the fibre of \(R^q i_* F\) at the point \(y_\infty\) at infinity of \(\mathbb{P}^1\) in the closed fibre.

Now it suffices (VII 3.3 and IX 2.9 (iii)) to treat the case where \(F\) is constructible. Then since \(\delta(F) \leqslant d\), there exists a closed subscheme \(X\) of \(\mathbb{P}^1\) with \(\dim X \leqslant d\) such that \(X\) contains the support of \(F\). Let \(\operatorname{Spec} A = \tilde{X}\) be the strict localization of \(X\) at the point \(y_\infty\), let \(\tilde{U} = \tilde{X} - \tilde{X} \times_{\mathbb{P}^1} Y_\infty\), and let \(\tilde{F}\) be the sheaf induced by \(F\) on \(\tilde{U}\). Note that \(U\) is obtained from \(\tilde{X}\) by localizing with respect to an element \(x \in \Gamma(X, \mathcal{O}_X)\). We have \[(R^q i_* F)_{y_\infty} \simeq H^q(\tilde{U}, \tilde{F}).\] It thus suffices to prove that \(H^q(\tilde{U}, F) = 0\), if \(q > d\), for each torsion sheaf \(\tilde{F}\) on \(\tilde{U}\).

We may now apply IX 5.6, with \(\varphi = \delta\), and we find that it suffices to prove that \[H^q(V, \mathbb{Z}/\ell) = 0 \quad \text{if} \quad q > \delta(V)\] for each \(V\) finite and integral over \(\tilde{U}\) and for \(\ell\) invertible. Let \(\pi : \bar{V} \to V\) be the normalization of \(V\). We have the exact sequence \[0 \longrightarrow (\mathbb{Z}/\ell)_V \longrightarrow \pi_*(\mathbb{Z}/\ell)_{\bar{V}} \longrightarrow C \longrightarrow 0\] with \(\delta(C) < \delta(V)\), and we deduce from this (by induction on \(\delta\)) that it suffices to take \(V\) normal.

Let \(B\) be the normalization of \(A\) in the field of rational functions on \(V\). Then \(B\) is an excellent strictly local ring of equal characteristics, and \(V\) is an affine open of \(\operatorname{Spec} B\), obtained by localizing with respect to \(x\). Let \(\hat{B}\) be the completion of \(B\), and \(\hat{V}\) the induced open (which is obtained from \(\operatorname{Spec} \hat{B}\) by localizing with respect to the image of \(x\) in \(\hat{B}\)). By 4.3, we have \[H^q(V, \mathbb{Z}/\ell) \simeq H^q(\hat{V}, \mathbb{Z}/\ell).\] We are thus reduced to proving that \[H^q(\hat{V}, \mathbb{Z}/\ell) = 0 \quad \text{if} \quad q > \delta(V) = \dim B = \dim \hat{B}.\] By the induction hypothesis, the theorem is true if \(\delta(V) < d\), so Theorem 6.1 bis applies in this situation. Consequently, it suffices to treat the case \(\dim \hat{B} = d\), and since \(\hat{B}\) is normal, we are in the situation of the lemma, whence the result.

6.7.0. We shall first prove 6.6 under additional hypotheses, in the case where \(B\) is of characteristic \(p > 0\). Let \(A\) be an equidimensional, complete ring of equal characteristics and let \(k \subset A\) be a field such that \(A/\operatorname{rad} A\) is a finite extension of \(k\). We say that the \(k\)-algebra \(A\) is formally separable if there exists a \(k\)-subalgebra of \(A\) of the form \(k[[x_1, \ldots, x_n]]\) such that the morphism \(\operatorname{Spec} A \to \operatorname{Spec} k[[x]]\) is finite and étale at the generic point of \(\operatorname{Spec} k[[x]]\) (\(x=(x_1, \ldots, x_n)\)).

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 6.7

Let \(k \subset B\) be a field over which \(B/\operatorname{rad} B\) is finite. Under the induction hypothesis on \(d\) above, the conclusion of 6.6 holds if the hypotheses of 6.6 are satisfied and if, moreover, one or the other of the following conditions is satisfied:

(i) \(k\) is of characteristic \(0\).

(ii) There exists an element \(x \in \operatorname{rad} B\) which is invertible on \(U\) and such that \(\bar{B} = B/(x)\) is a formally separable \(k\)-algebra.

Proof. Let us choose elements \(x_1 = x, x_2, \ldots, x_d\) of \(\operatorname{rad} B\) such that \(\{x_1, \ldots, x_d\}\) generates an ideal primary to \(\operatorname{rad} B\). Then \(B\) is a finite \(A\)-algebra, where \(A = k[[x_1, \ldots, x_d]]\), and \(\bar{B}\) is the \(k[[x_2, \ldots, x_d]] = \bar{A}\)-algebra \(B/x_1 B\). Since in case (ii) \(\bar{B}\) is analytically separable, in this case we can choose the elements \(x_2, \ldots, x_d\) in such a way that \(\bar{B}\) becomes a generically étale \(k[[x_2, \ldots, x_d]]\)-algebra. Then it follows immediately that \(B\) is likewise a generically étale \(A\)-algebra, which is also true, of course, in case (i).

Let \(b \in B\) be an element which generates the field extension \(R(B)\) over \(k((x))\). Let \(\varepsilon \in k[[x]]\) be the discriminant of the irreducible monic equation of \(b\) over \(k[[x]]\). In case (ii), we may choose \(b\) so that \(x_1\) does not divide \(\varepsilon\). Let us moreover write \(\operatorname{Spec} B - U = V(x_1) \cup Y\), where \(Y\) contains no irreducible component of \(V(x_1)\). Let \(C\) be the ring \(\Gamma(Y, \mathcal{O}_Y)\), where \(Y\) is taken with its reduced induced structure. By changing the \(x_2, \ldots, x_d\) if necessary, we may assume that \(V(x_d)\) is not contained in the image of \(Y\) in \(\operatorname{Spec} A\), and that moreover in case (ii) \(V(x_d)\) is not contained in \(V(\varepsilon)\).

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 6.8

Let \(A_0 = k[[x_1, \ldots, x_{d-1}]]\{x_d\}\) be the strict localization of \(k[[x_1, \ldots, x_{d-1}]][x_d]\) at the point \(x_1 = x_2 = \cdots = x_d = 0\). Under the above conditions, there exist an \(A^0\)-algebra \(B^0\), an affine open \(U^0 \subset \operatorname{Spec} B^0\), and an isomorphism \(A \otimes_{A^0} B^0 \simeq B\) such that the open of \(\operatorname{Spec} B\) induced by \(U^0\) is \(U\).

The proof of this lemma is analogous to that of 1.5: it suffices to find \(A^0\)-algebras \(B^0\), \(C^0\) and isomorphisms \(A \otimes_{A^0} B^0 \simeq B\), \(A \otimes_{A^0} C^0 \simeq C\), because then there will exist ([3] 1.4) a unique (surjective) morphism \(B^0 \to C^0\) inducing the morphism \(B \to C\). We therefore take \(U^0 = \operatorname{Spec} B^0 - \{(\operatorname{Spec} C^0) \cup V(x_1)\}\), and one sees immediately that \(U\) is induced by \(U^0\). The existence of \(C^0\), and of \(B^0\) in case (ii), is proved as in 1.5. The existence of \(B^0\) in case (i) is a consequence of ([3] 5.1). (It can also be proved directly by applying Abyankhar's lemma to the ramification along \(\{x_1 = 0\}\), and descent.)

We can now complete the proof of 6.7. By applying 4.3 once more, we find that \[H^q(U, \mathbb{Z}/\ell) \simeq H^q(U^0, \mathbb{Z}/\ell),\] from which it follows that it suffices to prove that this last group is zero for \(q > d\). Now \(\operatorname{Spec} A^0\) is a limit of affine schemes étale over \(k[[x_1, \ldots, x_{d-1}]][x_d]\), so \(\operatorname{Spec} B^0\) is a limit of schemes of finite type over \(\operatorname{Spec} k[[x_1, \ldots, x_{d-1}]]\) each of whose fibres is of dimension \(\leqslant 1\). Since \(U^0 \subset \operatorname{Spec} B^0[1/x_1]\), we have \[U^0 = \varprojlim U^0_\alpha\] where \(U^0_\alpha\) is affine of finite type over the scheme \(V^0 = \operatorname{Spec} k[[x_1, \ldots, x_{d-1}]][1/x_1]\) and where each fibre of \(U^0_\alpha/V^0\) is of dimension \(\leqslant 1\).

Let \(f^0 : U^0 \to V^0\) be the structural morphism. Since the fibres of \(f^0_\alpha\) are all of dimension \(\leqslant 1\), we have for \(v \in V^0\) \[\delta(\mathbb{Z}/\ell, f^0_\alpha, v) \leqslant \dim \mathcal{O}_{V^0,v} + 1 \leqslant d-1\] (because \(\dim \mathcal{O}_{V^0,v} \leqslant d-2\)). The induction hypothesis on \(d\) is therefore applicable to the morphism \(f^0\), and we find, by applying 6.1, \[R^q f^0_{\alpha*}(\mathbb{Z}/\ell) = 0 \quad \text{at the point } v \text{ if } q > \dim \mathcal{O}_{V^0,v} + 1,\] i.e. if \(q > d - \dim \bar{v}\). Thus \(R^q f^0_{\alpha*}(\mathbb{Z}/\ell) \neq 0\) at the point \(v\) implies that \(\dim \bar{v} \leqslant d-q\). Thus for the inclusion \[i : V^0 \longrightarrow \operatorname{Spec} k[[x_1, \ldots, x_{d-1}]] \quad (\text{cf } (6.0))\] we have \[\delta(R^q f^0_{\alpha*}(\mathbb{Z}/\ell)) \leqslant d-q,\] and the induction hypothesis, in the form 6.1 bis, applied to the morphism \(i\), implies that \[H^p(V^0, R^q f^0_{\alpha*}(\mathbb{Z}/\ell)) = 0 \quad \text{if} \quad p+q > d.\] The Leray spectral sequence \[E_2^{pq} = H^p(V^0, R^q f^0_{\alpha*}(\mathbb{Z}/\ell)) \Longrightarrow H^{p+q}(U^0, \mathbb{Z}/\ell)\] therefore implies that \(H^n(U^0_\alpha, \mathbb{Z}/\ell) = 0\) if \(n > d\), and since \(U^0\) is the limit of the \(U^0_\alpha\), we find likewise that \[H^n(U^0, \mathbb{Z}/\ell) = 0 \quad \text{if} \quad n > d.\]
This completes the proof of 6.7, hence of Theorem 6.1 in characteristic 0.

blocks.html: 7. Affine morphisms - end of the proof.
Recall that to complete the proof of 6.1 in characteristic \(p > 0\) (always under the resolution hypothesis), we had reduced, by 6.6, to proving the following assertion for \(d \geqslant 2\):

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 7.1

Let \(B\) be a complete local ring, normal, of equal characteristics, with separably closed residue field, and of dimension \(d\). Let \(U \subset \operatorname{Spec} B\) be an affine open such that there exists \(x \in \operatorname{rad} B\) which is invertible on \(U\). Then \[H^q(U, \mathbb{Z}/\ell) = 0 \quad \text{if} \quad q > d.\]
Moreover, by the induction hypothesis, we may assume that 6.1 is true for the values of \(\delta < d\), and that 7.1 has already been proved in the special case 6.7 (ii).

First, note that the condition that \(B\) be normal is not important. Indeed, let \(B\) be arbitrary, let \(\pi : \bar{B} \to B\) be the normalization of \(B\), and let \(\bar{U} \subset \operatorname{Spec} \bar{B}\) be the inverse image of \(U\). We have an exact sequence \[0 \longrightarrow (\mathbb{Z}/\ell)_U \longrightarrow \pi_*(\mathbb{Z}/\ell)_{\bar{U}} \longrightarrow C \longrightarrow 0,\] where the dimension of the support of \(C\) is \(< d\), so \(H^q(U,C) = 0\) if \(q > d-1\). Since \(H^q(U, \pi_*) = H^q(\bar{U},.)\) (VIII 5.6), we see that \[(7.2)\qquad \begin{aligned} H^q(U, \mathbb{Z}/\ell) &= 0 \quad \text{if} \quad q > d \quad \text{is equivalent to} \\ H^q(\bar{U}, \mathbb{Z}/\ell) &= 0 \quad \text{if} \quad q > d. \end{aligned}\]

7.3.0. We shall briefly recall, without proof, some properties of the notion of formal separability that we need. The reader may consult (EGA IV 18.11.10, 18.11.11): Let \(A\) be a complete noetherian local \(k\)-algebra whose residue field is a finite extension of \(k\), and denote by \(A'\) the completion of the local ring \(A \otimes_k k'\) (where \(k' = k^{1/p}\)). Then the extension \(A \to A'\) is radicial (possibly infinite), as one easily sees — this is the well-known example of Nagata. It is therefore harmless, for the computation of étale cohomology, to replace \(A\) by \(A'\) (VIII 1).

Now the condition on an equidimensional algebra \(A\) of dimension \(d\) of being formally separable, that is, of being a generically étale finite extension of \(k[[x_1,\ldots,x_d]]\), is expressed in terms of the module \(\hat{\Omega}^1_{A/k}\) (EGA IV 18.11.10), or of the Jacobian criterion (EGA \(\mathrm{O}_{\mathrm{IV}}\) 22.6, IV 7.1) (∗), and we see that if \(A\) is not analytically separable, then the \(k'\)-algebra \(A'\) is not reduced. One may, for example, reduce the proof to the case where \(A\) is given by an equation \(f = 0\), \(f \in k[[x_1,\ldots,x_{d+1}]]\), and apply the Jacobian criterion and the following lemma, whose pleasant proof we leave to the reader:

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 7.3

Let \(f(x_1,\ldots,x_n) \in k[[x_1,\ldots,x_n]]\) be a formal power series. Suppose that for each \(i = 1,\ldots,n\) there exists an invertible element \(u_i \in k[[x_1,\ldots,x_n]]\) such that \(u_i f\) is a series in \(x_i^p\) and in \(x_1,\ldots,x_{i-1},x_{i+1},\ldots,x_n\). Then there exists an invertible element \(v \in k[[x_1,\ldots,x_n]]\) such that \[vf \in k[[x_1^p, \ldots, x_n^p]].\]

It follows easily that by applying finitely many times the procedure of replacing \((A,k)\) by \((\bar{A}',k')\), where \(\bar{A}'\) is the normalization of \(A'\), we reduce to the situation where \(A\) is indeed formally separable. Likewise, one can prove that for a given \(x \in \operatorname{rad} A\), the ring \((A/(x))_{\text{red}}\) will become a formally separable algebra by the same procedure, applied to the algebra \(A\).
By applying VIII 1.1 and 7.2, we find

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 7.4

It suffices to prove (7.1) under the additional condition that \(B\) contains a field \(k\) over which \(B/\operatorname{rad} B\) is finite, and such that the \(k\)-algebra \((B/(x))_{\text{red}}\) is formally separable.
The proof of 7.1 in this case consists of a reduction to the special case treated in 6.7 (ii):

With the notation of 7.1, 7.4, let \[D(x) = \sum_i r_i X_i\] be the divisor of \(x\), so that each \(X_i\) is a closed irreducible subscheme of \(\operatorname{Spec} B\) of codimension 1 which is formally separable over \(k\) (that is, such that \(B/\mathfrak{J}(X_i)\) is a formally separable \(k\)-algebra, which is moreover equivalent to the assertion that \((B/(x))_{\text{red}}\) is formally separable). Let us choose \(y \in \operatorname{rad} B\) such that \[D(y) = \sum_i (r_i-1)X_i + \Gamma\] where \(\Gamma\) contains no \(X_i\), and consider the blow-up \[f : Z \longrightarrow \operatorname{Spec} B\] of the ideal \((x,y)\). The spectra of the rings \(B[y/x]\) and \(B[x/y]\) form an affine open covering of \(Z\).

Let \(B_1\) be the strict localization of \(B[x/y]\) at the maximal ideal generated by \((\operatorname{rad} B, x/y)\). For each closed point \(Q\) of the closed fibre of \(\operatorname{Spec} B[y/x] \to \operatorname{Spec} B\), denote by \(A_Q\) the strict localization of \(B[y/x]\) at \(Q\), and by \(U_Q\) the affine open of \(\operatorname{Spec} A_Q\) which is the inverse image of \(U\).

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 7.5

To prove 7.1 for the ring \(B\), it suffices to prove that for \(q > d\) (\(\geqslant 2\)) we have

(i) \(\quad H^q(\operatorname{Spec} B_1[y/x], \mathbb{Z}/\ell) = 0\)

and

(ii) \(\quad H^q(U_Q, \mathbb{Z}/\ell) = 0\) for each \(Q\).

Proof. We have open immersions \[U \hookrightarrow \operatorname{Spec} B[1/x] \hookrightarrow \operatorname{Spec} B[y/x],\] hence a diagram \[\xymatrix@R=2.2em@C=1.2em{ U \ar[rr]^-{i} \ar[dr]_{k} & & \operatorname{Spec} B[y/x] \ar[dl]^{j} \\ & Z & }\] If \(Q\) is a closed point of the closed fibre of \(\operatorname{Spec} B[y/x] \to \operatorname{Spec} B\), we have \((R^q i_* \mathbb{Z}/\ell)_Q = 0\) if \(q > 0\), by hypothesis. For each point \(P\) of \(\operatorname{Spec} B[y/x]\) which is not closed in the closed fibre of \(\operatorname{Spec} B[y/x] \to \operatorname{Spec} B\), we have \(\delta(F,i,P) < d\), where \(F = (\mathbb{Z}/\ell)_U\) (notation of (6.0)). Thus by applying the induction hypothesis and 6.1 to the morphism \(i\), we find that for the morphism \(\operatorname{Spec} B[y/x] \to \operatorname{Spec} B\) we have \[\delta(R^q i_* \mathbb{Z}/\ell) \leqslant d-q.\] Consequently, the induction hypothesis in the form 6.1 bis, applied to this last morphism, implies that \[H^p(\operatorname{Spec} B[y/x], R^q i_* \mathbb{Z}/\ell) = 0\] if \(q > 0\) and \(p > d-q\). With the Leray spectral sequence \[E_2^{pq} = H^p(\operatorname{Spec} B[y/x], R^q i_* \mathbb{Z}/\ell) \Longrightarrow H^{p+q}(U, \mathbb{Z}/\ell),\] we reduce, for the proof of 7.1, to proving that \[H^p(\operatorname{Spec} B[y/x], i_* \mathbb{Z}/\ell) = 0 \quad \text{if} \quad p > d.\]

We have an exact sequence \[(7.6)\qquad 0 \longrightarrow \mathbb{Z}/\ell \longrightarrow i_*(\mathbb{Z}/\ell)_U \longrightarrow C \longrightarrow 0\] where \(\delta(C) < d\). It therefore suffices (again by induction) to prove that \[(7.7)\qquad H^p(\operatorname{Spec} B[y/x], \mathbb{Z}/\ell) = 0 \quad \text{if} \quad p > d.\]

Now the open immersion \(\operatorname{Spec} B[y/x] \xrightarrow{\ j\ } Z\) is obtained by removing from \(Z\) the closed subset \(C\) "at infinity", and, in the other open \(\operatorname{Spec} B[x/y]\) of \(Z\), it is identified with the open \(C = V(x/y)\). The \(R^q j_* \mathbb{Z}/\ell\) are concentrated on \(C\), and the morphism \(C \to \operatorname{Spec} B\) is a closed immersion. Consequently, we have \(H^p(Z, R^q j_* \mathbb{Z}/\ell) = 0\) if \(p\) and \(q > 0\). Since the closed fibre of \(Z \to \operatorname{Spec} B\) is of dimension 1 and this morphism is proper, XII 5.3 bis implies that \(H^p(Z, j_* \mathbb{Z}/\ell) = 0\) if \(p > 2\). The spectral sequence \[E_2^{pq} = H^p(Z, R^q j_* \mathbb{Z}/\ell) \Longrightarrow H^{p+q}(\operatorname{Spec} B[y/x], \mathbb{Z}/\ell)\] therefore yields isomorphisms \[H^q(\operatorname{Spec} B[y/x], \mathbb{Z}/\ell) \simeq H^0(Z, R^q j_* \mathbb{Z}/\ell) \simeq (R^q j_* \mathbb{Z}/\ell)_P\] if \(q \geqslant 2\), where \(P\) is the point "at infinity" of \(Z\). These fibres are none other (VIII 5) than \[(R^q j_* \mathbb{Z}/\ell)_P \simeq H^q(\operatorname{Spec} B_1[y/x], j_* \mathbb{Z}/\ell).\]

By 7.7, it therefore suffices to prove that these last groups are zero if \(q > d\) (\(\geqslant 2\)). We have an exact sequence analogous to 7.6 which, together with the induction hypothesis, shows that it suffices that \[H^q(\operatorname{Spec} B_1[y/x], \mathbb{Z}/\ell) = 0 \quad \text{if} \quad q > d,\] whence the lemma.
Proof of 7.5 (i).

Consider the closed set \(C = V(x/y)\) of \(\operatorname{Spec} B[x/y]\), with the reduced induced structure. One sees immediately that the closed immersion of \(C\) into \(\operatorname{Spec} B\) induced by the morphism \(Z \to \operatorname{Spec} B\) identifies \(C\) with the closed subscheme \(X = \bigcup X_i\) of \(\operatorname{Spec} B\). Since \[\begin{aligned} D(x) &= \sum r_i X_i \\ D(y) &= \sum (r_i-1)X_i + \Gamma, \end{aligned}\] the element \(x/y\) generates the ideal \(\mathfrak{J}(X_i)\) locally at the generic point of \(X_i\), where the local ring is a discrete valuation ring because \(B\) is normal. Consequently, the morphism \(\operatorname{Spec} B[x/y] \to \operatorname{Spec} B\) is an isomorphism in a neighbourhood of such a point, and the element \(x/y\) vanishes to order 1 on each of the irreducible components \(C_i\) (corresponding to \(X_i\)) of \(C\).

Since the closed set \(C\) lifts to \(\operatorname{Spec} B_1\), this remains true if we replace the ring \(B[x/y]\) by \(B_1\), so \(B_1/(x/y)\) is a complete ring which is a formally separable \(k\)-algebra.

To prove 7.5 (i), we may first apply 4.3, which allows us to replace \(B_1\) by its completion \(\hat{B}_1\), which does not affect the ring \(B_1/(x/y)\). By 7.2, we may moreover replace \(\hat{B}_1\) by its normalization \(\bar{B}_1\). Since \(B_1\) (hence \(\hat{B}_1\)) is already regular at the generic points of the \(C_i\), the morphism \(\operatorname{Spec} \bar{B}_1 \to \operatorname{Spec} \hat{B}_1\) is an isomorphism at these points, so \(\bar{B}_1/(x/y)\) is again a formally separable \(k\)-algebra. We are thus reduced to the special case 6.7 (ii), whence the result.
Proof of 7.5 (ii).

Let us choose the point \(Q\) of the closed fibre of \(\operatorname{Spec} B[y/x] \to \operatorname{Spec} B\). The strict localization \(A_Q\) is written as a limit \[A_Q = \varinjlim A\] where \(A\) runs over a filtered category of étale rings of finite type over \(B[y/x]\). Let \(U_A\) be the affine open of \(\operatorname{Spec} A\) which is the inverse image of \(U\). Since \(x\) is invertible on \(U_A\), the morphism \(U_A \to \operatorname{Spec} B\) is étale, and \(U_A\) is normal. Consequently, if we denote by \(C\) the normalization of \(B\) in the field \(R(A)\) of rational functions on \(A\), we have an open immersion \[U_A \longrightarrow \operatorname{Spec} C.\]

It suffices (VII 5.7) to prove that for each \(A\), the image of \(H^q(U_A, \mathbb{Z}/\ell)\) in \(H^q(U_Q, \mathbb{Z}/\ell)\) is zero if \(q > d\). Since \(x\) is invertible on \(U_Q\), the morphism \(U_Q \to \operatorname{Spec} A\) factors through \(\operatorname{Spec} A[1/f]\), if \(f \in B\) is an arbitrary element such that \(f\) is divisible by \(x\) in \(B[y/x]\) and \(f/x\) does not vanish at the point \(Q\). It thus suffices to prove that for a suitable such \(f\), we have \[H^q(U_{A,f}, \mathbb{Z}/\ell) = 0 \quad \text{if} \quad q > d,\] where \(U_{A,f} = U_A - V(f)\) is the affine open of \(\operatorname{Spec} A[1/f]\), which is also an affine open of \(\operatorname{Spec} C\).

Let \(c \in k\) be an element such that \(y/x + c\) does not vanish at \(Q\), and let \(J\) be the ideal in \(B\) of the closed set \(\Gamma \cap X\). Then if \[(7.8)\qquad f \equiv y + cx \quad (\bmod J^N) \qquad N > 0,\] the element \(f\) satisfies the above condition: Indeed, one sees immediately that in \(\operatorname{Spec} B[y/x]\) we have \(V(J) = V(x)\). Thus (7.8) does imply that \(f\) is divisible by \(x\), whence \[f/x \equiv y/x + c \quad (\bmod J).\] Since \(J\) vanishes at \(Q\), and \(y/x + c\) is not zero at \(Q\), this proves our assertion.

Now \(\Gamma \cap X\) is a closed subset of \(\operatorname{Spec} B\) of codimension 2. Consequently, we may choose an \(f\) satisfying (7.8), call it \(z\), such that \(V(z) \cap V(y)\) is likewise of codimension 2. Let us also choose elements \(x_3, \ldots, x_d\) such that \(y,z,x_3, \ldots, x_d\) is a system of parameters of the ring \(B\). Then \(B\), hence also \(C\), is a finite \(k[[y,z,x_3, \ldots, x_d]]\)-algebra.

Let \(C^0\) be the normalization of \(k[[y,z,x_3, \ldots, x_d]]\) in the separable closure of \(k((y,z,x))\) in the field of rational functions \(R(C)\), so that \(C\) is a radicial extension of \(C^0\), and \(C^0\) is a generically étale extension of \(k((y,z,x))\) (where \(x = x_3, \ldots, x_d\)).

Let us choose a linear combination \[f = az + by \qquad (a,b \in k),\] such that the morphism \[\operatorname{Spec} C^0 \longrightarrow \operatorname{Spec} k[[z,y,x]]\] is étale over the generic point of \(V(f)\), and such that \(f/x\) does not vanish at \(Q\) in \(\operatorname{Spec} B[y/x]\). It suffices to prove that \[H^q(U_{A,f}, \mathbb{Z}/\ell) = 0 \quad \text{if} \quad q > d,\] hence (VIII 1.1) to prove that \[H^q(U^0_{A,f}, \mathbb{Z}/\ell) = 0 \quad \text{if} \quad q > d,\] where \(U^0_{A,f}\) is the open of \(\operatorname{Spec} C^0\) corresponding to the open \(U_{A,f}\) of \(\operatorname{Spec} C\), which is an affine open, as one sees by descent (EGA IV 2.7.1 (xiii)). But by construction, the element \(f\) of \(C^0\) is invertible on \(U^0_{A,f}\), and \(C^0/(f)\) is a formally separable \(k\)-algebra. We are therefore in the situation of 6.7 (ii), which completes the proof of 7.5 (ii), hence of 6.1.
